html:
The fossil skull of a child, about three years old, found in 1924 at a limestone quarry near Taung in South Africa. The anatomist Raymond Dart described it in 1925 and named a new species, Australopithecus africanus, "the southern ape of Africa". It is now thought to be between two and three million years old.

The skull had a small, ape-sized brain but human-like teeth, and the hole for the spinal cord showed it walked upright. Dart argued it was a human ancestor and that humans had evolved in Africa, as Charles Darwin had guessed.

Most experts rejected him for decades. They expected a large brain to have come first, and they were misled by the fake Piltdown Man. Finds by Robert Broom and others, and later Lucy in Ethiopia, proved Dart right. A study in 2006 suggested the child was killed by a large bird of prey. The site is now part of a World Heritage Site for human origins.
